questions.question: A payment API call times out, so the client retries the identical charge request; the customer is billed exactly once because the server deduplicates retries. Which property makes repeating the call safe?
questions.explanation: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether performed once or many times.

questions.question: A 2003-era application calls an old DLL function that no longer exists, so the vendor ships a thin compatibility layer translating those calls to the new API. What is that layer called?
questions.explanation: A shim is a small adapter translating calls made for an old interface to the new one.

questions.question: Callers need one simple start() method, but the subsystem behind it juggles ten interdependent classes; the team adds a single front class that hides that complexity. Which design pattern is this?
questions.explanation: A facade exposes a simplified interface over a complex subsystem.

questions.question: A reviewer finds a 900-line method with six parameters named a1 through a6 — not a bug yet, but a surface hint of deeper design rot. What is such a hint called?
questions.explanation: A code smell is a surface symptom hinting at deeper structural problems.

questions.question: Process A holds the file lock while waiting for the printer lock; Process B holds the printer lock while waiting for the file lock — neither can ever proceed. Name this concurrency bug.
questions.explanation: Deadlock is circular waiting on resources so that all involved processes block forever.

questions.question: Two threads each read balance=100, each add 50, and each write 150 — one deposit silently vanishes only when timing interleaves badly. Name this class of bug.
questions.explanation: A race condition makes correctness depend on uncontrollable timing between concurrent operations.

questions.question: A checkout service emits 'OrderPlaced' without knowing who listens; email, inventory, and billing services each react independently. Which messaging pattern is this?
questions.explanation: Pub-sub decouples event producers from consumers through a brokered topic.

questions.question: When the primary database node dies, the cluster promotes a replica and traffic shifts within seconds with no operator action. What is this automatic switch called?
questions.explanation: Failover is the automatic switch to a standby component when the primary fails.

questions.question: A bad deploy corrupts user records, so ops restores the database to last night's snapshot, returning the system to a known-good state. What is this restoration called?
questions.explanation: A rollback reverts a system to a previous good state after a failed change.

questions.question: A release goes live for only 2% of users on one server while error metrics are watched before a wider rollout. Which deployment strategy is this?
questions.explanation: A canary release exposes changes to a small user slice first — like a canary in a coal mine.

questions.question: Instead of patching servers in place, the team bakes a fresh machine image, replaces every instance wholesale, and discards the old ones. Name this approach.
questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure replaces rather than mutates servers, eliminating configuration drift.

questions.question: A shipping API starts timing out, so the calling service stops sending it requests for 60 seconds and fails fast, giving the dependency room to recover instead of drowning it. Which resilience pattern is this?
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker halts calls to a failing dependency, failing fast until it recovers.

questions.question: A flood of traffic from thousands of infected devices knocks a website offline; what attack is this?
questions.explanation: A DDoS attack overwhelms a target with traffic from a botnet, making the service unavailable.

questions.question: A hospital's files suddenly carry .locked extensions while a screen demands Bitcoin for the decryption key — and the backups were wiped first. Name this attack class.
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts victim files and extorts payment for the decryption key.

questions.question: Attackers exploited a flaw the same week it was discovered; the vendor had not yet shipped a fix, so no patch existed to apply. What is such a vulnerability called?
questions.explanation: A zero-day is exploited before the vendor has had any days to issue a patch.

questions.question: An attacker overwhelms a server by starting thousands of TCP handshakes that are never completed, exhausting its connection queue. Name this specific flood attack.
questions.explanation: A SYN flood sends SYN packets without the final ACK, filling the server's half-open connection table and blocking real users.

questions.question: A user's passwords appear in stolen logs even though they typed them only into legitimate sites; a hidden program had recorded every keystroke. Which malware class is this?
questions.explanation: Keyloggers silently capture keyboard input to harvest credentials, messages, and other typed data.

questions.question: After a breach, auditors find every password hashed with plain MD5, so identical passwords share identical hashes. Which practice of adding random data to each password before hashing was skipped?
questions.explanation: A per-password salt makes each hash unique, defeating rainbow tables and shared-hash lookups.

questions.question: A bank transfer must either debit one account and credit the other completely, or change nothing at all if any step fails. Which ACID property guarantees this all-or-nothing behavior?
questions.explanation: Atomicity makes a transaction indivisible: every step commits together or the whole transaction rolls back.

questions.question: A web app crashes after an attacker submits an input far longer than expected, spilling past its allocated memory and overwriting adjacent data. Name this vulnerability class.
questions.explanation: Missing bounds checks let writes exceed the buffer, corrupting memory and often enabling code execution.
